newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Russia and the West split over Serbia policy.
newsitem.headline: Russia and the West split over Serbia policy.

text.p: A split emerged between Russia and the West over policy towards Serbia as Moscow warned against outside interference in the Balkan republic while Washington, Paris and Bonn backed Belgrade's anti-government reformers.

The major power jockeying came as opposition street protests against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic entered their sixth week in response to his ruling party's annulment of opposition victories at municipal elections last month.

About 100,000 people ignored snow and freezing temperatures to demonstrate in Belgrade on Wednesday, a day after violent clashes between surging crowds of Milosevic supporters, opposition marchers and police sent in to seprate them.
Among those still hospitalised after Tuesday's running street battles was a man shot in the head and critically wounded by a Milosevic supporter.

Milosevic, widely viewed as the instigator of the Croatian and Bosnian wars, saw his reputation somewhat rehabilitated in 1995 when Europe and the United States relied on him to help broker and implement a Bosnian peace deal.
But Washignton and Paris accused him of sparking Tuesday's violence by busing his supporters into Belgrade for a rally at the same time and place as an opposition demonstration.

More than a month of demonstrations went off peacefully before Milosevic and his SPS party staged the counter-protest, an event which fell flat when only 40,000 supporters showed up compared to several hundred thousand opposition marchers.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel warned that any further violence would jeopardize Serbia's efforts to integrate with Europe.
Moscow took a different tack. Russia's Foreign Ministry issued a statement branding outside attempts to interfere in Serbian politics as "inadmissibale".

The Russian comment was clearly aimed at Western efforts to pressure Milosevic into relaxing his grip on the media, police and judiciary -- a stranglehold which has given him dictatorial control over public life in Serbia.
Russia and the West were often at odds during the Bosnian war, sometimes working at cross-purposes in their efforts to contain and finally end the conflict.

Milosevic and his Bosnian Serb allies exploited the divisions, especially those between Moscow and Washington, to buy time and territory for Serb military forces and to shield them from NATO retaliation.

Milosevic is now apparently counting on Moscow to prevent the West from using the U.N. Security Council to reimpose economic sanctions which were lifted earlier this year in the wake of the Bosnian peace agreement.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is expected to present its findings on the deteriorating political situation in Serbia within the next week.
Zoran Djindjic, leader of the opposition Democratic Party, warned that Milosevic and the SPS might be preparing to ban opposition marches in Belgrade, a move he vowed would be ignored on the streets.
